stimulus:
A clock doesn't really measure time; it counts the stutters of a thing that wants to unwind. The mainspring pushes, and the escapement says no, not yet, then yes, a little. That tick is a tiny act of rationing. The anchor escapement rocks back and forth, catching teeth on a wheel, and the sound is the wheel slamming into a brake over and over. Time as a controlled series of collisions.

Which makes me think of pendulums, and Galileo supposedly watching a swinging lamp in Pisa, though that story smells embroidered. Anyway, a pendulum's period depends on length, not weight, so a clock runs slow in summer when the brass rod expands. Hence Harrison's gridiron pendulum, bars of two metals fighting each other's expansion so the net length stays put. Cancellation as craftsmanship.

Then there's the longitude problem, where a wobbly ship made pendulums useless, so he built springs and balance wheels that ignored gravity's direction. Sailors' lives hung on a watch not noticing the sea.

Quartz does the same job with a vibrating crystal at 32,768 hertz, a number chosen because it's two to the fifteenth, so fifteen halvings give one pulse per second. Binary hiding inside your wristwatch. Meanwhile atomic clocks count cesium's jitter, and the second is officially a pile of 9,192,631,770 cycles. Oddly specific, like a phone number for eternity.

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Gridiron-style compensation: paired AP-1 factor perturbation
ideas.description: Harrison's gridiron cancels opposing expansions, so a memory readout should be robust to nuisance drift. Acutely degrade or inhibit AP-1 (e.g., dTAG degron of FOS/JUN, dominant-negative A-FOS) at different times after a priming stimulus, then quantify chromatin accessibility and transcriptional response on restimulation. Compare this against a counter-perturbation that boosts the opposing factors, to show that AP-1 is needed specifically to maintain the primed state and not just to induce it.

ideas.title: Escapement-style pulse-train stimulation with live AP-1 reporters
ideas.description: A clock converts a steady force into discrete ticks, so test how AP-1 responds to pulsed versus sustained stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or growth factor pulses of varied frequency and spacing). Track FOS/JUN dynamics live with endogenous knock-in reporters, and ask whether the response to a second pulse depends on the interval since the first. A decay time constant that lasts days after the stimulus is gone would support memory.

ideas.title: Single-cell multiome tracking of AP-1 motif accessibility across a prime–rest–restimulate time course
ideas.description: Run scATAC and RNA-seq at baseline, after priming, after a long rest, and after restimulation. Use chromVAR and footprinting to ask whether AP-1 binding sites opened by priming stay open during rest and whether they predict faster or stronger gene induction. Link this to cell lineage barcodes, so that heritable memory across divisions can be separated from persistence in non-dividing cells.

ideas.title: Quartz-style halving test: memory persistence through cell division
ideas.description: Quartz divides a fixed frequency down to a countable beat. In the same way, follow primed cells through a defined number of divisions, using dye dilution or a division-tracking reporter. Measure AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) and the primed response after 0, 1, 2 and more divisions. Check whether memory halves with each division, which would indicate dilution, or is stably re-established, which would indicate a self-propagating mechanism.

ideas.title: Sufficiency test with synthetic AP-1 site editing and transient pioneer-like recruitment
ideas.description: Use CRISPR to mutate or insert AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or to recruit dCas9–FOS/JUN transiently, then remove the trigger. Measure whether enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac and enhanced gene induction persist after AP-1 is gone. Persistence would show AP-1 can write memory. Loss of memory when only the motifs are mutated would show the sites are necessary.
